newsitem.title: CANADA: Directors, options said behind Arakis resignations.
newsitem.headline: Directors, options said behind Arakis resignations.

text.p: Rifts over the membership of Arakis Energy Corp's board of directors and compensation for work leading to the company's US$1.0 billion Sudan oil deal led to the resignations of three company vice-presidents, one of the executives who quit said on Friday.

"A big part of it had to do with our view of what should be the makeup of the board of directors moving forward," David Robinson, who was an Arakis executive vice-president until Thursday, said in an interview.
"We felt that there needed to be a number of independent outside directors brought into the company from within the oil industry and elsewhere."

Robinson said calls from the resigning trio, which also included Arakis vice-president of corporate relations David Harrison and executive vice-president Peter Holstein, for an expanded board "were not taken seriously" by the company's management and current directors.

Arakis's four-director board includes chairman Lutfur Khan, known for his connections with the Sudanese government, and John McLeod, the company's chief executive who was brought in to lead the firm following the collapse last year of a debt deal that would have financed the Sudan project.
Robinson said there remained a perception that Arakis was still run by the same people who were at the helm "during last year's debacle," and that was pressuring its stock price.
Robinson, Harrison and Holstein, all well known to many of the company's investors, resigned on Thursday after a long and tumultuous period for Arakis and its shareholders.

The company in early December announced a joint venture deal with the China National Petroleum Corp, Petronas and the Sudan government to develop the 12.2 million acre Arakis oil concession is southern Sudan and build a 950-mile pipeline to the Red Sea.
Robinson also said that a dispute between the three executives and Arakis management over how options were allocated played a role in the resignations.

The executives, and especially Holstein, had played major roles in bringing to the table potential joint venture partners for the Sudan deal, which had not been recognized in the form of more options granted to trio in 1996, Robinson said.
He said he disputed what he called "the company's spin" that the three executives were merely financial and investor relations employees.
